course.title: Dartmouth BASIC (1964)
course.description: Learn the original BASIC from Dartmouth College, step by step.
course.note: The original used the arrow ↑ for powers. On modern keyboards we write ^ instead.

lessons.title: Hello, 1964
intro: In 1964, John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz at Dartmouth College created BASIC so that every student could use a computer, not just scientists.
A BASIC program is a list of numbered lines. The computer always runs them from the lowest number to the highest, no matter in which order you typed them.
PRINT shows something on the screen. Text goes between quotes. END marks the end of the program and must always be the last line.

exercises.explanation: PRINT shows the text between the quotes. The quotes themselves and the line number are not printed.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line so it shows HI THERE.
exercises.explanation: PRINT is the BASIC statement for output.

exercises.prompt: Why does every line start with a number?
options: It sets the order in which the lines run
It counts how often the line runs
exercises.explanation: Line numbers define the order. Programmers usually count in steps of 10 (10, 20, 30) so they can insert new lines later, e.g. 15.

exercises.prompt: Put the lines in the order the computer runs them.
exercises.explanation: The computer sorts by line number, no matter in which order you typed them.

exercises.prompt: One line breaks the rules. Tap it.
exercises.explanation: In Dartmouth BASIC, END must be the last line, with the highest line number. Here line 30 comes after END.

options: ONE TWO THREE (each on its own line)
ONE THREE TWO (each on its own line)
exercises.explanation: Line 20 runs before line 30, even though it was written below it. Each PRINT starts a new line.

lessons.title: Variables with LET
intro: A variable is a named box that stores a number. You can put a number in, read it later, and change it whenever you want.
You fill a variable with LET. In the original 1964 BASIC, LET was required; later versions made it optional.
Variable names are very short: one letter (A) or one letter followed by one digit (A1, X9). Names like AB or SUM are not allowed.

exercises.explanation: LET assigns a value to a variable. In the original BASIC, LET was required.

exercises.prompt: Which one is NOT a valid variable name in Dartmouth BASIC?
exercises.explanation: Names are one letter, or one letter plus one digit. AB has two letters, so it is not allowed.
PRINT calculates the expression first: 3 + 4 = 7.
LET X = X + 1 takes the old value (5), adds 1, and stores the result back in X.
In the original Dartmouth BASIC you had to write LET A = 5. Later dialects made LET optional.
A starts at 5, is doubled to 10, then printed.

lessons.title: Calculating
intro: BASIC knows the usual math operators: + (add), - (subtract), * (multiply), / (divide) and ^ (to the power of).
The order is the same as in school: powers first, then * and /, then + and -. Parentheses change the order, and whatever is inside them is calculated first.
BASIC works with decimal numbers, so 10 / 4 gives 2.5, not 2.

exercises.explanation: Multiplication comes first: 3 * 4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14.
Parentheses first: 2 + 3 = 5, then 5 * 4 = 20.
^ means 'to the power of': 2 * 2 * 2 = 8. The 1964 original used the arrow ↑ for this.
BASIC works with decimal numbers, so 10 / 4 is 2.5, not 2.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the area of a rectangle (length times width).
exercises.explanation: Area = length * width = 6 * 4 = 24.

exercises.prompt: Build a program that prints the average of 4 and 8.
exercises.explanation: (4 + 8) / 2 = 6. Without parentheses, BASIC would calculate A + B / 2 = 4 + 4 = 8.

lessons.title: Talking to the Screen
intro: PRINT can show several things in one line. A semicolon ; prints the next item directly after the previous one. A comma , jumps to the next column, which is handy for tables.
You can mix text and numbers: PRINT "X IS "; X shows the text and then the value of X.
A semicolon at the very end of a PRINT line keeps the cursor on the same line, so the next PRINT continues there.
REM stands for 'remark'. The computer ignores everything after it, so you can leave notes for yourself and other humans.

options: A and B on separate lines
exercises.explanation: A semicolon prints the next item directly after the previous one, without a gap.

exercises.prompt: What does the comma do in this line?
options: Jumps to the next column, leaving a gap
Prints a comma between the words
exercises.explanation: The comma moves to the next print zone (a fixed column), which lines things up like a table.

exercises.prompt: Make the computer show HELLO on one line.
exercises.explanation: A semicolon at the end of a PRINT keeps the cursor on the same line, so line 20 continues right after HEL.
Text in quotes is printed as-is. X without quotes is a variable, so its value 7 is printed.

options: Nothing, it is a note for humans
exercises.explanation: REM lines are remarks. The computer skips them completely.

exercises.prompt: This program stops with ?MISSING QUOTE. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explanation: Line 10 opens a quote but never closes it. Text always needs a quote at the start and at the end.

exercises.prompt: Build a program that prints AREA = 12.
exercises.explanation: First store both sides, then print the text followed by the calculated area: 4 * 3 = 12.
